Is the new focus on monetization hurting games?

I'm actually kinda split on this. On the one hand, I appreciate the advent of free-to-play games (dirty bomb, gotham city impostors, TF2, and a shit ton of mobile games). I get them with the understanding that they will be good for a little casual fun and for that I will need to put up with annoying micro-transactions.

ON THE OTHER HAND

Major AAA titles that have moved to the pay-to-win or "here's a game, but if you want it all, you need to pay for the DLC subscription" make me sick. I didn't pay $50-60 to be nickle and dimed once I have the game. And I will make decisions on purchasing a game specifically on this criteria. Dead Space 3 is a good example of how a game company can screw a game up with in-game purchases and the reaction it can have in the community.

I feel like the pendulum has swung to the monetization side, but with the backlash from consumer, I think there is a chance it could swing back to the other side soon, so long as we all vote with our wallets.

This is why I think companies should probably start charging more for their game. Instead of nickle and dimming, just flat out release a game at, lets say $75 - $80 - Maybe even $100. That way you don't have to worry about doing things like splitting up the community. I personally feel like people would actually pay that price if they were A) Getting a good complete game at release B) Actually getting all content releases that could possibly be planned for the game.

These companies are companies with people. While I understand the need to nickle and dime, it is a double edge sword to these businesses. They are destroying and splitting up the consumers that they very much rely on.
All that will end up happening then is we get 80$-100$ games and dlc... they wont stop doing one lucrative thing just because they do another.

Video games are evolving as a business. They are trying to find the best way to monetize their games and its up to the customer to push them in the right direction.

I like Destiny as the perfect example of this because it straddles so many different worlds an tries to break new ground.

Console gamers are not very accustomed to the monthy subscription model of MMOs. They want to buy the game and play it until they tire of it. You can throw in some DLC or expansions and some people will buy them but not everyone. This effectively fractures your player base and leaves many people behind. You can't have this with a 'living world' like Destiny. As the game expands the players must move forward.

BungiVision took the middle road and cut out the monthy fee most MMOs have and decided to do a console friendly DLC schedule. The problem was that they had two groups of players in their community, RPG players and FPS players, who expected different things from DLC. RPG players expected WoW type expansions whereas FPS players did not. RPG players knew that if you didn't keep current on expansions you would be left behind and the game would cease to be 'playable' FPS players had no idea this was a thing. So they got shit on from both sides with every expansion.

So how do they monetize their IP? Most players won't tolerate monthy charges on top of their Xbox Live and PS plus fees and quarterly DLC leaves too many people behind and eventually destroys the community. That leaves one option. Microtransactions.

If they can get the most 'devoted' players to subsidize the cost of development for the rest of the player base then everyone wins. The playerbase no longer gets fractured by DLC, they avoid a monthy fee and reap the goodwill from the players because the microtransactions don't affect gameplay.

Its already been shown by games like Team Fortress 2, League of Legends and many others that if you make a good game people enjoy playing they will spend money on the dumbest shit possible and subsidize those who free-ride.

Even Halo is doing it now and I like it.

I think this is the future of monetization in video games. Whether or not there is an initial purchase required we'll start seeing microtransactions in nearly every game. The question remains will players put up with games where the micrtransactions advantage the purchasers over the free-riders and I think it will depend on the initial investment of the player. Most people don't like the idea of paying for a game then paying again to be competitive in that game but we'll see.

Dead Space 3 is a good example of how a game company can screw a game up with in-game purchases and the reaction it can have in the community.

Well, I don't think the focus on monetization is really new, per se. But yes, the recent status quo that seems to have set in whereby developers release unfinished or hacked-up games at full price, only to release the missing content for purchase later, complete with bugfixes that can only be acquired by purchasing said content, is fucking detestable. Look at what happened to Destiny: content that was available on release is now locked behind a paywall; you literally have to purchase a content patch in order to continue enjoying the game in the fashion you were enjoying it prior to the release of the content patch.

Eh, there will always be a battle between art and monetization of it, the usual philosophy is that good games will sell well, but with micro transactions and day 1 DLC that has proven to not be the case everytime.

Where AAA games have failed a good portion of indie games have picked up thr pieces and have made some incredible video gaming experiences.

The biggest loser of modern monetization is MMORPGs in my opinion. Indie budgets simply can't make a decent game of that scale and stupid AAA companies desperately want WoW numbers, ending up with a plethora of shitty WoW clones that flop in a month. The only decent big budget MMO is Eve and even that came close to collapsing.

Monetization is ok but fragmenting a came is not. Destiny is a fragmented game, if you don't buy the new expansions you get into a fragmented section of the community that cannot participate in some aspects of the game. Weekly raids, daily bonuses, you are shown exactly where the company thinks you are. The bottom.

As far as e-sports, COD is doing this in AW by using expansion maps for competitions. In the old days, only maps that came with the game could be used. Pro's played those maps and were rewarded for their expertise. Now they are rewarded depending on how much money they pay. This also creates a small paywall which is arguably minute, when you add the amount they get from each purchase you quickly realize it's actually a lot of money.

Online passes ultimately kill the used and borrowed game market. Which can make older games which stressed incredible online play (bf3 or twisted metal) essentially worthless. This makes trade ins worthless as well.

Micro transactions can be argued based upon how much your time is worth. If someone was payed 10$ an hour and a 10$ item cut their grind by 1 hour then can be argued as useful. If a 10$ item cuts the grind by 10 minutes then the balance is off, the micro transactions themselves aren't bad. Developers make them bad. WOT is especially difficult to play for free, many vehicles requiring high cost ammunition in order to even penetrate enemy targets, with the highest tier vehicles being quite obviously unprofitable from an in game standpoint. Switching or obtaining new crews is incredibly expensive if you do it a lot. Which you need to because 6th sense is needed on everything. If you are a fan of a F2P game, they usually have sales and whatnot. If your paying attention it actually can be quite cheap.

Monetizing should allow us to have better games with more features and better gameplay. Whats hurting games is the fact that people keep preording games for 100$ that turn out to be shit, and then do the same the next month. If gamers stopped pre ordering games and not paying to win, only paying for content thats truly worth it, the AAA titles will soon adjust. When you know im not gonna pay shit unless the game is finished, youre sure as hell going to finish the game before you release it. Im no more free of guilt than anyone else, but its definitely our fault that we let them get away with it, not their fault for milking their golden cows
